title: SALD: Self-Referenced Advantage Learning for Diffusion Models

paper.title: SALD: Self-Referenced Advantage Learning for Diffusion Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Recent work on language-model adaptation has shown that single models can obtain informative training signals by evaluating their behavior in demonstration- or feedback-augmented contexts, with the help of a teacher network, which is driven by the students’ learned parameters. Inspired by this internal-reference principle, we investigate how diffusion models can identify self-referenced training signals without external demonstrations or teacher networks. We introduce SALD, a self-referenced training framework that evaluates each image-caption pair at two noise levels using the same model. The easier, lower-noise path is evaluated without gradient tracking to provide a reference, while the harder, higher-noise path provides the training gradient. Rather than directly distilling the easy-path prediction, SALD uses the difference between two path errors to adapt the hard-path objective. The proposed Advantage-Guided Diffusion (AGD) converts this relative error into a differentiable sample-level weight. Temporal Advantage Memory (TAM) accumulates relative difficulty across training and adapts the future gap between the two noise levels. Spectral Advantage Decomposition (SAD) further compares the residual power spectra of the two paths and constructs a differentiable, frequency-derived latent-element weight. All components share a single set of model parameters, requiring neither an external teacher network nor additional trainable parameters during training or inference, and no modification to the inference procedure. Experiments across multiple architectures and datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in generation quality, while component-wise ablations quantify the contributions of the proposed components.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion Ho et al. (2020) ; Song et al. (2020) and flow-matching Lipman et al. (2022) ; Albergo et al. (2025) based generative models have become standard backbones for high-fidelity image synthesis, with Diffusion Transformers further improving scalability and generation quality Peebles and Xie (2023) . In parallel, recent work on language-model adaptation has shown that a model can obtain richer online training signals by evaluating its behavior under additional information. Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning conditions a self-teacher on expert demonstrations, whereas Self-Distillation Policy Optimization conditions a self-teacher on feedback obtained from the model’s own attempts Shenfeld et al. (2026) ; Hübotter et al. (2026) . These approaches show that useful supervision can be constructed without relying on a stronger external teacher. Transferring this principle to diffusion training is not straightforward: diffusion models do not naturally receive textual demonstrations or retrospective feedback, and their training states are sampled from a prescribed corruption process rather than from autoregressive policy rollouts. Moreover, standard diffusion objectives still average gradients uniformly across training pairs and latent elements, although their difficulty varies substantially across images, captions, noise levels, and visual details Vincent (2011) ; Choi et al. (2022) . Neural networks also exhibit spectral bias, learning coarse low-frequency structure before fine high-frequency detail Rahaman et al. (2019) ; Wang and Pehlevan (2025a) . Consequently, uniform training can continue to emphasize already learned signals while underweighting examples and visual components that remain difficult. Can a diffusion model construct its own easier reference and use it to adapt training across harder examples, prompts, noise levels, and visual frequencies, without teachers, demonstrations, or feedback datasets? A unified answer remains missing because existing methods address only parts of this problem. Noise-level weighting Karras et al. (2022) ; Esser et al. (2024) ; Hang et al. (2025) adjusts training according to timestep or signal-to-noise ratio, but normally applies the same rule to all examples evaluated at a given noise level. Noise selection methods show that different noise instances provide unequal training signals Qi et al. (2024a) , but they do not maintain a persistent estimate of how the difficulty of an individual image-caption pair changes throughout training. Curriculum learning Bengio et al. (2009) orders examples by difficulty, but typically depends on a fixed or externally defined curriculum and are not adaptive noise selection. Distributionally robust optimization emphasizes difficult subpopulations Sagawa et al. (2019) , whereas frequency-aware objectives address spectral imbalance; neither directly combines the sample-level, temporal, and spectral difficulty in diffusion training. Likewise, demonstration- or feedback-conditioned language-model self-distillation cannot be transferred directly because diffusion training provides neither an in-context demonstration, nor a feedback-conditioned output distribution to distill Shenfeld et al. (2026) ; Hübotter et al. (2026) . These limitations motivate a self-referenced diffusion objective in which an easier view of the same training pair provides a relative difficulty signal rather than a teacher prediction target. We introduce SALD, which evaluates every image-caption pair at two noise levels using one shared model: an easier low-noise path and a harder high-noise path. The easy path is evaluated without gradient tracking and serves as an internal reference, while model parameters are updated through the hard path. SALD does not directly distill the easy-path prediction into the hard path. Instead, it measures the increase in weighted prediction error from the easy path to the hard path and uses this relative signal to adapt the hard-path objective. Advantage-Guided Diffusion (AGD) converts the scalar error difference into a normalized, differentiable sample weight, emphasizing training pairs whose error grows under the harder condition. Temporal Advantage Memory (TAM) maintains an exponential moving average of relative difficulty for every training pair and uses it to adapt future noise-level gaps, forming a continuous per-example curriculum Bengio et al. (2009) . Spectral Advantage Decomposition (SAD) compares the residual power spectra of the two paths and constructs a differentiable, frequency-derived latent-element weight, providing a finer training signal related to spectral bias Rahaman et al. (2019) ; Wang and Pehlevan (2025a) . All components reuse the same set of model parameters and require neither a teacher network nor additional trainable model parameters during training or inference. The method introduces no change to the inference procedure. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce AGD, a self-referenced weighting mechanism that estimates sample importance from the relative error between hard and easy noise paths, without any teachers, demonstration datasets, or architectural changes. • We introduce TAM and SAD to extend relative difficulty across training history and spectral structure, enabling an adaptive per-example noise curriculum and frequency-derived, latent-element weighting. • We characterize the optimization behavior of the resulting differentiable weighting objective and evaluate SALD across multiple architectures and datasets. The experiments demonstrate consistent gains in generation quality, while component-wise ablations quantify the contributions of AGD, TAM, and SAD.

sections.heading: 2 Proposed Approach
sections.text: The same diffusion model evaluates each image-caption pair at two noise levels. The lower-noise evaluation forms an easy path , which is computed without gradient tracking and serves as an internal reference. The higher-noise evaluation forms a hard path , through which the model parameters are updated. By comparing these paths, SALD addresses three questions: (i) Which examples are currently difficult? (ii) How large should the easy-to-hard noise gap be for each example? and (iii) At which frequencies does the hard-path residual remain large? Advantage-Guided Diffusion (AGD), Temporal Advantage Memory (TAM), and Spectral Advantage Decomposition (SAD) address these questions, respectively. All components share the same model parameters; therefore, SALD requires neither an external teacher nor an additional trainable model during training or inference. Figure 2: SALD framework. A frozen VAE encodes the input latent, processed through two paths: Low-Noise Path A (w/o gradient) and High-Noise Path B (with gradient). AGD computes an advantage for sample reweighting, while TAM stabilizes it via per-sample EMA, forming a persistent curriculum across timestep gaps. SAD compares FFT power spectra of velocity residual maps, applies a sigmoid gate, and reconstructs a spatial weight map via IFFT to focus gradients on high-frequency error regions. Together, these define ℒ SALD \mathcal{L}_{\text{SALD}} for adaptive gradient allocation across samples.

The only stopped branches are the easy-path references. TAM is stored as a non-trainable state and is not backpropagated through time. SALD uses two forward evaluations, but only the hard evaluation stores a backward graph. For this reason, the method is more precisely described as self-referenced advantage learning than as teacher-student self-distillation.

We evaluate generated images using Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) Heusel et al. (2018) , CLIP score Radford et al. (2021) , and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) Zhang et al. (2018) . FID measures distributional similarity to real images (quality and diversity). CLIP score captures alignment with text prompts, while LPIPS assesses perceptual similarity, together evaluating fidelity, semantics, and realism. FID is computed using the Inception-V3 network with 2048-dimensional pool features. CLIP Score is computed using the CLIP ViT-L/14 model from OpenAI. LPIPS is computed using a VGG backbone. Further details are mentioned in Appendix D.1 .

sections.heading: 3.2 Ablation Study
sections.text: We conduct an ablation study using SANA 0.6B on COCO 2017 ( × 512 512\!\times\!512 ) and MAGICK ( × 1024 1024\!\times\!1024 ), using the uniform flow-matching baseline as the reference across all cases. Case 1: Individual Contributions. AGD contributes most strongly among individual components, as direct difficulty-aware reweighting provides an immediate training signal. SAD offers complementary gains through spectral routing, improving structural fidelity at the cost of modest CLIP degradation. TAM alone yields the weakest improvement, since its EMA-based memory requires a sustained difficulty signal from AGD to stabilise, a notable limitation when used in isolation. Together, all three components are necessary to close the full performance gap. Case 2: Pairwise Combinations. AGD+SAD achieves the best pairwise result, as the two components operate on complementary axes, sample difficulty, and spectral structure, without cross-dependency. TAM+SAD performs weakest among pairs, confirming TAM’s dependence on AGD’s advantage signal for effective curriculum updates. The SALD surpasses all pairs, demonstrating non-redundant synergy across components. Case 3: AGD Temperature τ \tau . Moderate sharpness ( τ = 0.5 \tau=0.5 ) best balances gradient focus and perceptual stability. Overly low τ \tau over-concentrates on extreme samples, slightly harming LPIPS, while high τ \tau degrades toward a near-uniform loss, weakening the difficulty signal. SALD exhibits a clear U-shaped sensitivity, with gains degrading at both extremes. Case 4: TAM EMA Decay α \alpha . The default α = 0.90 \alpha=0.90 strikes the best balance between curriculum responsiveness and stability. Aggressive decay ( α = 0.50 \alpha=0.50 ) introduces noisy difficulty estimates, while near-frozen memory ( α = 0.999 \alpha=0.999 ) fails to track the evolving training landscape. The wider performance spread on MAGICK confirms that longitudinal difficulty tracking is more critical at higher resolution, where sample complexity varies more sharply. Case 5: Maximum Noise Gap Δ max \Delta_{\max} . Both extremes degrade performance: a narrow gap ( Δ max = 100 \Delta_{\max}=100 ) weakens contrast between hard and easy paths, while an overly wide gap ( Δ max = 500 \Delta_{\max}=500 ) pushes the easy path into a near-noiseless regime, overestimating difficulty and destabilising training. The default Δ max = 250 \Delta_{\max}=250 yields the best results across both benchmarks, with a consistent U-shaped FID response confirming the sensitivity of the advantage signal to gap magnitude. Case 6: Core Design Decisions. All five choices prove critical. Absolute loss (no contrast): replacing A ( i ) = ℓ b ( i ) − sg ⁡ ( ℓ a ( i ) ) A^{(i)}=\ell_{b}^{(i)}-\mathrm{sg}(\ell_{a}^{(i)}) with | ℓ a ( i ) | |\ell_{a}^{(i)}| collapses gains toward the baseline, most severely at 1024 2 1024^{2} , confirming relative difficulty, not raw loss magnitude, as the effective signal. Fixed δ \delta (no ramp): removing the warm-up destabilises the advantage signal during early training, mildly degrading perceptual quality. Detach disabled: allowing w ( i ) w^{(i)} to backpropagate causes the model to exploit the weighting mechanism rather than improve predictions, validating sg ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathrm{sg}(\cdot) as non-negotiable. Reduced steps ( 12 12 vs. 20 20 ): SALD at 12 steps still outperforms the 20-step uniform baseline, indicating that training against the hard-to-easy trajectory yields a smoother learned flow with fewer steps required at inference. Cross-batch advantage: computing advantage relative to a second independently drawn batch rather than the same sample’s easier noise path yields partial gains but falls short of SALD, confirming that intra-sample noise contrast is a strictly stronger signal than inter-sample difficulty, which conflates sample hardness with distributional variation.

sections.heading: 4 Related Work
sections.text: Denoising diffusion models Ho et al. (2020) and score-based generative models Song et al. (2020) established iterative denoising as a powerful paradigm for image synthesis. Flow matching Lipman et al. (2022) ; Albergo et al. (2025) provides a continuous-time alternative by learning velocity fields along interpolation paths. Recent transformer-based generators, including DiT Peebles and Xie (2023) , rectified-flow transformers Esser et al. (2024) , SANA Xie et al. (2024) , PixArt- α \alpha Chen et al. (2023) , and PixArt- Σ \Sigma Chen et al. (2024) , further improve scalability and high-resolution generation. However, most objectives still treat samples, timesteps, and spatial locations uniformly. Several works improve training by reallocating the gradient budget across noise levels. EDM Karras et al. (2022) studies principled noise schedules and σ \sigma -weighting, while P2 Choi et al. (2022) emphasizes perceptually important SNR regions. Improved noise schedules Hang et al. (2025) and noise-instance analysis Qi et al. (2024a) further show that different noise levels and noise samples provide unequal training signals. These approaches define global timestep-dependent weights, whereas AGD computes per-sample relative difficulty from the loss gap between low- and high-noise paths. Our work is also related to curriculum learning Bengio et al. (2009) , self-paced learning Kumar et al. (2010) , dynamic instance hardness Chang et al. (2020) , adaptive curricula Kong and others (2021) , diffusion curricula Liang et al. (2025) , and adaptive point-weighting Li et al. (2025) . Hard-example mining Felzenszwalb et al. (2010) ; Shrivastava et al. (2016) and DRO Sagawa et al. (2020) ; Feoktistov et al. (2025) ; Ma et al. (2024) similarly emphasize difficult examples, while meta-hard mining Mu and others (2025) and coreset selection Killamsetty et al. (2021) select informative samples. Unlike these methods, TAM stores an EMA of relative advantage and uses it to adapt the timestep gap for each sample. Finally, SAD connects to spectral bias studies Rahaman et al. (2019) ; Xu et al. (2020) ; Wang and Pehlevan (2025b) and frequency-aware diffusion methods Benita et al. (2025) ; Si et al. (2024) ; Jiralerspong et al. (2025) ; Esteves and Makadia (2026) ; Liu et al. (2025) . Instead of modifying the architecture, sampler, or noising process, SAD uses contrastive spectral residuals to construct spatial importance weights for loss reweighting. Recent work uses feedback-conditioned output distribution to distill Shenfeld et al. (2026) ; Hübotter et al. (2026) from teacher to student in the language domain but requires demonstration example and EMA based teacher. The proposed model can be seen as distillation from easy to hard sample, however it does not requires extra copy of the model parameters.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented SALD, a unified training framework for flow-based diffusion models that reallocates gradient budget across samples, noise levels, and frequency components. AGD estimates relative sample difficulty by contrasting losses between low and high-noise states, producing normalized within-batch importance weights. TAM extends this signal across the training set through persistent per-sample memory, enabling an adaptive curriculum over timestep gaps. SAD further refines optimization by converting contrastive spectral residuals into frequency-derived latent weights, emphasizing frequency patterns that remain under-learned. Since only the easy-path reference is detached, SALD preserves the original prediction target while improving where and how training effort is applied. In general, SALD offers a simple, architecture-agnostic approach for improving diffusion training without modifying the model, sampler, or inference procedure. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets and architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, while theoretical analysis supports the empirical findings.

sections.heading: Appendix A Why Is Uniform Training Suboptimal?
sections.text: The standard flow-matching loss used in Section 2.1 averages the losses of all training samples and all elements of their latent residuals. Apart from the time-dependent factor w ⁡ ( t ) w(t) , it assigns the same explicit coefficient to every sample and latent element. This does not mean that all samples produce equal gradients; samples with larger residuals can naturally produce larger gradient magnitudes. Rather, the objective has no explicit mechanism for adapting a sample’s importance according to its current difficulty or for distinguishing the frequency content of its remaining residual. This uniform treatment leads to two limitations that can become more important as training progresses, especially during domain-specific fine-tuning. The first limitation is at the sample level. Not all images are equally difficult for the current model. A clean portrait against a plain background may be learned early, after which its loss becomes small and further updates provide limited new information. Meanwhile, a cluttered street scene with reflections, thin text, and overlapping objects may remain difficult for much longer. Under uniform weighting, both samples retain the same explicit coefficient in the mini-batch objective, even though reallocating more emphasis to the difficult sample may be more useful. Prior work on hard-example mining and diffusion-noise selection similarly shows that examples and noise realizations can provide unequal training value Shrivastava et al. (2016) ; Qi et al. (2024b) . Consequently, uniform weighting can spend part of the finite optimization budget on already well-learned samples while under-emphasizing examples that remain difficult. The second limitation concerns the frequency content of the residual within each image. Deep networks are known to learn low-frequency content faster than high-frequency content, a behavior referred to as spectral bias or the frequency principle Rahaman et al. (2019) ; Xu et al. (2020) . Related frequency-dependent behavior has also been studied in diffusion models Yang et al. (2023) ; Si et al. (2024) ; Wang and Pehlevan (2025a) . Smooth structures such as skies and walls may be reconstructed earlier, whereas fine details such as hair strands, feather textures, specular highlights, and small text can lag behind. However, the standard mean-squared error collapses the full latent residual into a single scalar and does not explicitly indicate which frequency bands retain comparatively large error. Importantly, frequency magnitude does not identify the spatial locations of those errors because the power spectrum discards Fourier phase. The relevant goal is therefore to identify difficult frequency components and use them to construct a frequency-derived latent weight, rather than to claim a localized pixel-level error map. One natural idea is curriculum learning Bengio et al. (2009) ; Kumar et al. (2010) , in which easy samples are shown first and harder samples are introduced later. Classical curricula, however, often rely on a fixed notion of difficulty. In diffusion training, a sample’s difficulty changes as the model improves, so a static ordering can quickly become stale. What is needed instead is a strategy that (i) measures which samples become difficult relative to the current model when noise is increased, (ii) remembers this relative difficulty across training steps, and (iii) identifies which residual frequencies remain difficult. Unlike demonstration- or feedback-conditioned language-model self-distillation Shenfeld et al. (2026) ; Hübotter et al. (2026) , SALD constructs its reference from two noise states of the same image–caption pair: a lower-noise easy path evaluated without gradient tracking and a higher-noise hard path that supplies the training gradient. Advantage-Guided Diffusion (AGD) performs differentiable sample-level reweighting, Temporal Advantage Memory (TAM) maintains persistent relative-difficulty estimates and adapts future noise gaps, and Spectral Advantage Decomposition (SAD) constructs a frequency-derived latent weight. These components share one set of model parameters and require no external teacher or additional model copy during training or inference.

sections.heading: Appendix D Additional Results
sections.text: In this section, we present additional qualitative and quantitative results to further analyze SALD’s behavior across different datasets, architectures, and training settings. We include extended visual comparisons and supplementary experiments that highlight the contributions of AGD, TAM, and SAD to generation quality, optimization stability, and fine-grained detail preservation. Algorithm 1 summarizes a single SALD training step. Given a mini-batch of image–caption pairs, we first determine a base noise-level gap using a simple curriculum: during warm-up, the gap increases from 1 1 to Δ \Delta , after which it is sampled uniformly from { 1 , … , Δ } \{1,\ldots,\Delta\} . This base gap is then modulated for each sample using Temporal Advantage Memory (TAM), which scales the gap according to the sample’s stored difficulty score and clips it to the valid range. For each example, we sample a lower-noise easy level and obtain the corresponding higher-noise hard level by adding the TAM-adjusted gap. Two noisy views of the same latent are then constructed using independent Gaussian perturbations. The same model performs two forward passes: the easy path is evaluated under no_grad and serves as an internal reference, whereas the hard path remains differentiable and supplies the training gradient. From the residuals of these two paths, Spectral Advantage Decomposition (SAD) compares their frequency-domain error magnitudes and maps a zero-phase spectral gate back to the latent coordinates to obtain a frequency-derived weighting kernel. Since this construction does not retain the residual phase or recover the locations of the original errors, the kernel should not be interpreted as a localized pixel-level advantage map. Instead, it reweights the hard-path residual loss using the relative spectral errors of the two paths. In parallel, Advantage-Guided Diffusion (AGD) defines the sample advantage as the difference between the differentiable hard-path loss and the stop-gradient easy-path reference loss. It converts this advantage into a normalized sample weight that emphasizes harder examples within the batch. Finally, TAM stores the numerical advantage for future visits to the sample; the memory is non-trainable, and no gradient is propagated through this state update. The SALD objective is then formed by averaging the sample-weighted SAD losses of the hard paths before backpropagation. In this way, the algorithm adapts the training signal across samples, noise levels, and spectral components through a dynamic, self-referenced curriculum. sections.heading: D.2 Wall-Clock Evaluation
sections.text: We further evaluate the training efficiency of SALD under a matched wall-clock budget. As shown in Table 5 , SALD incurs approximately 25 % 25\% additional wall-clock time per training step compared with the corresponding baseline, measured on the same NVIDIA RTX A6000 setup. This overhead comes from the additional easy noise reference path: SALD performs gradient computation and backpropagation only for the hard noise path, while the easy noise path is evaluated without gradient computation, requiring only an additional forward pass. To account for this overhead, SALD is trained for 10 10 k steps, while the baselines are trained for 12.5 12.5 k steps. Thus, the total training budgets are approximately matched, since 10 ​ k × 1.25 ≈ 12.5 ​ k 10\text{k}\times 1.25\approx 12.5\text{k} . As reported in Table 5 , under this comparable wall-clock budget, SALD consistently achieves better generation quality across both CUB-200 and MultiGen datasets. In particular, SALD improves FID, CLIP, and LPIPS over the corresponding baseline models across all evaluated backbone configurations. These results show that the limited additional cost introduced by the no-gradient reference path is compensated by SALD’s faster convergence, allowing it to achieve superior generation quality within approximately the same overall training time as the baselines.

sections.heading: D.3 Impact of Inference Steps and Model Scalability
sections.text: Table 6 reveals a consistent sampling-efficiency advantage of SALD across model scales, from SANA 0.6B/1.6B to PixArt- Σ \Sigma 0.6B, on Oxford Flowers. As the number of inference steps is reduced, SALD preserves generation quality more effectively than the corresponding Base models, yielding lower FID and LPIPS while retaining comparable or higher CLIP scores. In particular, for both SANA models, SALD at 15 steps attains lower FID than the Base model at 20 steps (30.60 vs. 33.11 for SANA 1.6B and 25.54 vs. 30.64 for SANA 0.6B), using 25% fewer sampling steps, although LPIPS and CLIP at 15 steps remain slightly below the 20-step Base values. The behavior is consistent with the relative error signal introduced in Eq. 6 . Instead of treating prediction errors at different noise states independently, SALD contrasts the hard and easy states of the same sample and assigns greater importance when the harder state exhibits a larger error. Through the AGD weighting in Eq. 7 , optimization therefore concentrates on trajectory regions where prediction remains comparatively difficult. This encourages more accurate learning of the velocity field along challenging portions of the noise trajectory, which in turn reduces the dependence on densely spaced inference updates. The cross-scale results in Table 6 suggest that this effect is not specific to a particular architecture size, but translates into consistently stronger quality–efficiency trade-offs across the evaluated models. Furthermore, Figure 8 provides a qualitative view of this faster inference-time convergence using SANA 1.6B trained on DALL ⋅ \cdot E 3 1M. The distinction is most pronounced at low sampling budgets. SALD establishes the correct facial structure and overall appearance within the first few steps, with the 10-step output already closely resembling its 15- and 20-step generations. In contrast, the baseline remains highly unstable at 5 and 10 steps, exhibiting substantial changes in geometry, illumination, and color before converging toward a consistent image at later steps. Thus, additional sampling primarily refines the SALD output rather than correcting its global structure, whereas the baseline requires more iterations to stabilize both structure and appearance. This visual progression further supports that SALD learns a more efficient generation trajectory, allowing coherent samples to emerge under substantially fewer inference steps. sections.heading: D.4 What happens if we train 10 × \times More?
sections.text: To examine whether the gains reported at the main training budget are a consequence of insufficient training of the Baseline, we extend both the Baseline and SALD models to 100 100 k training steps, corresponding to 10 × 10\times the standard 10 10 k-step training budget. Table 7 reports the results across SANA 1.6B and SANA 0.6B on the MultiGen and Oxford 102 Flowers datasets. SALD maintains a consistent FID advantage over the corresponding Baseline throughout the extended training horizon, while CLIP and LPIPS remain comparable. For example, at 10 10 k steps, SALD already achieves substantially lower FID than the Baseline, reducing it from 26.44 26.44 to 23.86 23.86 on MultiGen and from 33.11 33.11 to 27.37 27.37 on Oxford 102 Flowers with SANA 1.6B. Importantly, this advantage does not disappear as training continues, demonstrating that the improvements observed at the main 10 10 k-step setting are not simply a consequence of under-training the Baseline. The extended training results also reveal diminishing returns at later stages of optimization. After approximately 80 80 k steps, both models improve more slowly. SALD maintains a clear FID advantage over the Baseline in this later regime: the gap remains stable on MultiGen ( 2.58 2.58 at both 10 10 k and 100 100 k for SANA 1.6B) and narrows but persists on Oxford 102 Flowers (from 5.74 5.74 to 3.71 3.71 for SANA 1.6B and from 4.81 4.81 to 3.57 3.57 for SANA 0.6B). Thus, extending training to 100 100 k steps does not eliminate the advantage of SALD. Instead, the results demonstrate that the gain introduced by SALD persists throughout the extended training process, while further optimization beyond 80 80 k steps provides only marginal improvements for either method. These observations support the use of 10 10 k steps as a practical training budget for the main experiments and confirm that the reported improvements are not due to premature termination of Baseline training.

sections.heading: D.5 Additional Visual Samples
sections.text: We provide additional visual samples generated by SALD across multiple datasets, architectures, and resolutions to analyze its ability to preserve semantic consistency, structural fidelity, and fine-grained visual details under diverse generation settings. Figure 6 presents qualitative comparisons between baseline finetuning and SALD across multiple architectures on the MAGICK and DALL ⋅ \cdot E 3 1M datasets at 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 resolution. Across all settings, SALD produces sharper and more structurally coherent generations with improved preservation of fine-grained semantic details. On MAGICK, baseline models often generate unstable crown geometry, distorted facial structure, inconsistent jewelry placement, and blurred ornamental details, whereas SALD maintains cleaner symmetry, sharper textures, and more realistic facial composition. Similarly, on DALL ⋅ \cdot E 3 1M, baseline generations exhibit inconsistent hand–object interactions, oversmoothed hair textures, and weaker illumination consistency around the magical orb. In contrast, SALD generates more stable anatomy, finer hair strands, improved lighting coherence, and stronger object-boundary preservation. These improvements are consistent across SANA and PixArt variants, demonstrating that SALD effectively enhances high-frequency detail generation and semantic consistency at high resolutions. Figure 7 further showcases diverse samples generated by SALD using PixArt- Σ \Sigma at 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 resolution on the DALL ⋅ \cdot E 3 1M dataset. Additionally, Figure 10 further showcases diverse samples generated by SALD using Flux.2 klein at 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 resolution on the DALL ⋅ \cdot E 3 1M dataset. The generated images demonstrate strong semantic consistency, realistic illumination, and preservation of fine-grained textures across a wide variety of scenes and subjects. In portrait generations, SALD maintains detailed facial structure, natural skin textures, and coherent lighting interactions. For reflective and transparent objects, such as the crystal sphere, the model accurately captures highlights, reflections, and depth cues. Indoor and environmental scenes exhibit consistent global composition and soft lighting transitions, while animal generations preserve high-frequency fur textures and sharp eye details. These results highlight the ability of SALD to generate visually coherent and high-fidelity images across diverse semantic categories at high resolution. Figure 11 presents qualitative generations produced by SALD across diverse datasets, resolutions, and backbone architectures, demonstrating both visual fidelity and semantic consistency. In the first row, SALD applied to SANA 1.6B trained on DALL ⋅ \cdot E 3 1M generates highly detailed urban neon scenes with realistic illumination effects, accurate text rendering, and strong spatial coherence at 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 resolution. The reflections on wet cobblestone surfaces and the natural bokeh distribution highlight the model’s ability to preserve fine-grained lighting structure and texture realism. The second row showcases generations on the CUB-200 dataset, where SALD captures intricate feather structures, wing symmetry, and motion-aware details in a snowy owl generated from an out-of-dataset prompt, while maintaining sharp focus on salient regions such as the eyes and plumage patterns. Finally, the third row demonstrates PixArt- Σ \Sigma generations on Oxford-102 Flowers, where SALD produces smooth petal geometry, subtle color gradients, and realistic depth-of-field effects with visually pleasing softness and fine texture retention. Across all settings, the generated samples exhibit strong compositional stability, high-frequency detail preservation, and improved prompt alignment, indicating that SALD generalizes effectively across both natural and artistic image domains.

sections.heading: Appendix E Limitations
sections.text: SALD evaluates each training example through two noise levels using the same diffusion model: the lower-noise easy path provides an internal reference under no_grad , whereas the higher-noise hard path supplies the training gradient. Consequently, SALD requires neither an external teacher nor additional trainable model parameters during training or inference. Nevertheless, the additional easy-path evaluation increases the per-step training cost by approximately 25 % 25\% . Although our wall-clock-matched experiments (Table 5 ) show that the resulting improvement in optimization efficiency can offset this overhead, reducing the per-step training cost remains an important direction for future work. One possibility is to cache easy-path reference predictions from earlier checkpoints. However, such cached predictions would become stale as the model changes and would depart from the formulation considered in this work, where the reference is always computed with the current model parameters. TAM stores one non-trainable scalar for each training sample. This memory cost is negligible for the dataset sizes considered in our experiments but grows linearly with the number of training examples. Moreover, TAM updates a sample’s memory only when that sample is revisited, so its curriculum effect is weaker when each example is seen only a few times during training. For extremely large web-scale datasets, group-level, clustered, or compressed difficulty statistics could reduce this cost and increase the update frequency, although such approximations may sacrifice the precision of the per-sample curriculum. Finally, our empirical evaluation is limited to fine-tuning pretrained text-to-image flow-matching models; we do not evaluate SALD for training from scratch. Our convergence analysis also holds only for a fixed TAM memory state (Remark 4). While we describe how the same easy–hard self-referencing principle can be extended to DDPM-style noise-prediction objectives, we do not experimentally validate that extension in this work. Evaluating SALD with noise-prediction models, in from-scratch training, and in other generative modalities, including video and 3D generation, remain directions for future research. Inspired by this internal-reference principle, we investigate how diffusion models can identify self-referenced training signals without external demonstrations or teacher networks. We introduce SALD, a self-referenced training framework that evaluates each image-caption pair at two noise levels using the same model. The easier, lower-noise path is evaluated without gradient tracking to provide a reference, while the harder, higher-noise path provides the training gradient. Rather than directly distilling the easy-path prediction, SALD uses the difference between two path errors to adapt the hard-path objective. The proposed Advantage-Guided Diffusion (AGD) converts this relative error into a differentiable sample-level weight. Temporal Advantage Memory (TAM) accumulates relative difficulty across training and adapts the future gap between the two noise levels. Spectral Advantage Decomposition (SAD) further compares the residual power spectra of the two paths and constructs a differentiable, frequency-derived latent-element weight. All components share a single set of model parameters, requiring neither an external teacher network nor additional trainable parameters during training or inference, and no modification to the inference procedure. Experiments across multiple architectures and datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in generation quality, while component-wise ablations quantify the contributions of the proposed components. Figure 1: Images generated by SALD using the SANA 0.6B model at a resolution of 1024 × 1024 1024	imes 1024 . 1 Introduction Diffusion Ho et al. (2020) ; Song et al. (2020) and flow-matching Lipman et al. (2022) ; Albergo et al. (2025) based generative models have become standard backbones for high-fidelity image synthesis, with Diffusion Transformers further improving scalability and generation quality Peebles and Xie (2023) . In parallel, recent work on language-model adaptation has shown that a model can obtain richer online training signals by evaluating its behavior under additional information. Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning conditions a self-teacher on expert demonstrations, whereas Self-Distillation Policy Optimization conditions a self-teacher on feedback obtained from the model’s own attempts Shenfeld et al. (2026) ; Hübotter et al. (2026) . These approaches show that useful supervision can be constructed without relying on a stronger external teacher. Transferring this principle to diffusion training is not straightforward: diffusion models do not naturally receive textual demonstrations or retrospective feedback, and their training states are sampled from a prescribed corruption process rather than from autoregressive policy rollouts. Moreover, standard diffusion objectives still average gradients uniformly across training pairs and latent elements, although their difficulty varies substantially across images, captions, noise levels, and visual details Vincent (2011) ; Choi et al. (2022) . Neural networks also exhibit spectral bias, learning coarse low-frequency structure before fine high-frequency detail Rahaman et al. (2019) ; Wang and Pehlevan (2025a) . Consequently, uniform training can continue to emphasize already learned signals while underweighting examples and visual components that remain difficult. Can a diffusion model construct its own easier reference and use it to adapt training across harder examples, prompts, noise levels, and visual frequencies, without teachers, demonstrations, or feedback datasets? A unified answer remains missing because existing methods address only parts of this problem. Noise-level weighting Karras et al. (2022) ; Esser et al. (2024) ; Hang et al. (2025) adjusts training according to timestep or signal-to-noise ratio, but normally applies the same rule to all examples evaluated at a given noise level. Noise selection methods show that different noise instances provide unequal training signals Qi et al. (2024a) , but they do not maintain a persistent estimate of how the difficulty of an individual image-caption pair changes throughout training. Curriculum learning Bengio et al. (2009) orders examples by difficulty, but typically depends on a fixed or externally defined curriculum and are not adaptive noise selection. Distributionally robust optimization emphasizes difficult subpopulations Sagawa et al. (2019) , whereas frequency-aware objectives address spectral imbalance; neither directly combines the sample-level, temporal, and spectral difficulty in diffusion training. Likewise, demonstration- or feedback-conditioned language-model self-distillation cannot be transferred directly because diffusion training provides neither an in-context demonstration, nor a feedback-conditioned output distribution to distill Shenfeld et al. (2026) ; Hübotter et al. (2026) . These limitations motivate a self-referenced diffusion objective in which an easier view of the same training pair provides a relative difficulty signal rather than a teacher prediction target. We introduce SALD, which evaluates every image-caption pair at two noise levels using one shared model: an easier low-noise path and a harder high-noise path. The easy path is evaluated without gradient tracking and serves as an internal reference, while model parameters are updated through the hard path. SALD does not directly distill the easy-path prediction into the hard path. Instead, it measures the increase in weighted prediction error from the easy path to the hard path and uses this relative signal to adapt the hard-path objective. Advantage-Guided Diffusion (AGD) converts the scalar error difference into a normalized, differentiable sample weight, emphasizing training pairs whose error grows under the harder condition. Temporal Advantage Memory (TAM) maintains an exponential moving average of relative difficulty for every training pair and uses it to adapt future noise-level gaps, forming a continuous per-example curriculum Bengio et al. (2009) . Spectral Advantage Decomposition (SAD) compares the residual power spectra of the two paths and constructs a differentiable, frequency-derived latent-element weight, providing a finer training signal related to spectral bias Rahaman et al. (2019) ; Wang and Pehlevan (2025a) . All components reuse the same set of model parameters and require neither a teacher network nor additional trainable model parameters during training or inference. The method introduces no change to the inference procedure. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce AGD, a self-referenced weighting mechanism that estimates sample importance from the relative error between hard and easy noise paths, without any teachers, demonstration datasets, or architectural changes. • We introduce TAM and SAD to extend relative difficulty across training history and spectral structure, enabling an adaptive per-example noise curriculum and frequency-derived, latent-element weighting. • We characterize the optimization behavior of the resulting differentiable weighting objective and evaluate SALD across multiple architectures and datasets. The experiments demonstrate consistent gains in generation quality, while component-wise ablations quantify the contributions of AGD, TAM, and SAD. 2 Proposed Approach The same diffusion model evaluates each image-caption pair at two noise levels. The lower-noise evaluation forms an easy path , which is computed without gradient tracking and serves as an internal reference. The higher-noise evaluation forms a hard path , through which the model parameters are updated. By comparing these paths, SALD addresses three questions: (i) Which examples are currently difficult? (ii) How large should the easy-to-hard noise gap be for each example? and (iii) At which frequencies does the hard-path residual remain large? Advantage-Guided Diffusion (AGD), Temporal Advantage Memory (TAM), and Spectral Advantage Decomposition (SAD) address these questions, respectively. The proposed model can be seen as distillation from easy to hard sample, however it does not requires extra copy of the model parameters. 5 Conclusion We presented SALD, a unified training framework for flow-based diffusion models that reallocates gradient budget across samples, noise levels, and frequency components. AGD estimates relative sample difficulty by contrasting losses between low and high-noise states, producing normalized within-batch importance weights. TAM extends this signal across the training set through persistent per-sample memory, enabling an adaptive curriculum over timestep gaps. SAD further refines optimization by converting contrastive spectral residuals into frequency-derived latent weights, emphasizing frequency patterns that remain under-learned. Since only the easy-path reference is detached, SALD preserves the original prediction target while improving where and how training effort is applied. In general, SALD offers a simple, architecture-agnostic approach for improving diffusion training without modifying the model, sampler, or inference procedure.
